->E P I S T L E<-

...that is, as a follower of **Aristotle** (of whom he was a most devoted student), he did not strictly maintain the **immortality of the soul** <note>original: "animi immortalitatem." Pomponazzi famously argued that while the soul's immortality is a truth of faith, it cannot be proven by reason or by the teachings of Aristotle.</note>, nor did he believe it could be fully defended through Aristotelian doctrine. Yet, as a **Christian**, he maintained that he did not disagree with the **Catholic Church**; he admits this quite clearly in this present work—one of his last—especially in the first and final chapters. He makes the same claim regarding true **miracles**. In order to defend these, he does not hesitate to repeatedly accuse his own beloved Aristotle, as well as **Plato** and other philosophers, of ignorance. He asserts that their teachings are insufficient and "blind" <note>original: "coecam"</note> when it relates to the miracles and religion of **Christ**, and the understanding of **God’s omnipotence**. ### PETRUS POMPONATIUS

<margin>
*Demons do not understand individuals through species.* <note>original: "Demones non intelligant singularia per species."</note>
</margin>

This position does not seem possible to sustain, because they would understand either through innate <term>innate: "congenitas," meaning knowledge they are born with rather than learned from experience.</term> species, or through species newly received. If they understand through innate species, these would be either universal—such that through the species of "man" they would distinctly know all individual men, and likewise for "donkey" and any other species—or they would have a distinct and separate species for each and every individual. 

The first of these options does not seem possible to assign. For if they knew all individuals through one and the same species (such as the category of "man"), they would then either know all individuals simultaneously, and thus know an infinite number of things distinctly, which does not seem admissible. In this way, a demon would know infinite things infinitely many times over, since there are almost infinite types of species, and within each species, infinite individuals—especially since he knows the present no more than the past and the future. 

If, however, through such a universal species <term>species: in scholastic philosophy, a "species" is the mental image or form that allows an intellect to recognize an object.</term> he were to know only *some* individuals, there is no way to provide a reasonable cause as to why—since that universal species applies equally to all <note>The text cuts off here, but Pomponazzi is arguing that a general concept like "humanity" shouldn't favor knowing Socrates over Plato.</note>

<summary>Pomponazzi argues that demons cannot know individuals through general concepts (species), because if they did, they would either have to know every individual across all time simultaneously (an impossible infinity) or have no logical reason to know one person but not another.</summary>

However, this does not seem possible to be argued reasonably: 

Firstly, because the demon's knowledge of Socrates would then not be something absolute, but something relative <note>original: "non esset quid absolutũ, sed quid respectiuũ." In scholastic logic, an "absolute" thing exists in itself (like a color), while a "relative" thing exists only in comparison to something else (like being "taller").</note>. That same knowledge would begin and cease to exist in the demon in the same way that equality, likeness, or any universal relation can begin or cease to exist for someone solely because of a change occurring in another. 

Hence, for a demon to know Socrates would be exactly as if Socrates became equal to Plato without any change having been made in Plato. This can by no means be said: for equality expresses nothing absolute, nor does it add anything real to quantity; whereas the knowledge of Socrates does the opposite. For knowledge is something real and something absolute.

But this I do know: that if what is applied toward health—induced thus by the demon's art—ought to be felt, it must be felt in both cases; for in both, it is a **natural operation**.

[Medicine] fails because of these **hidden properties** <note>original: "proprietates occultas." In Renaissance philosophy, these were qualities that could not be explained by the balance of the four humors (hot, cold, wet, dry) but were inherent to the specific nature of a thing.</note>; for some men have died from the administration of an **enema**, and some from **cassia** <note>A plant-based laxative common in medieval pharmacy.</note>, even though these were administered according to the rules of the medical art. Hence, **medicine** <term>medicina: Pomponazzi distinguishes between a "perfect science" (which deals with universal, unchanging truths) and medicine, which is often an "art" dealing with unpredictable individuals.</term> itself is not rendered a perfect science.

Since, therefore, the second mode arises from an **individual property**, it cannot fall within the scope of science. Nor even can the third mode, as is well enough known, because the **imaginative power** <term>vis imaginans: the faculty of the soul that forms mental images; it was believed by some to be capable of physically affecting one's own body or even the bodies of others.</term> does not produce such effects unless the person is predisposed to them; and very few such people are found. For they must possess many conditions, as the **Conciliator** <note>Pietro d’Abano (c. 1250–1316), a physician and philosopher who attempted to "reconcile" the differences between Greek and Arabic medical traditions.</note> says in the place cited, which rarely coincide in one person.

Truly, regarding these matters, a certain expertise and knowledge can be had only in a **universal** sense and not in the **particular**. For instance, [one might know] that some men perform this through a property acquired from the **principles of their generation** <note>original: "principijs generationis." This refers to the specific circumstances of a person's birth, including their biological makeup and the astrological influence at the time of conception or delivery.</note>; but it is similarly not knowable who these people are, or what kind of disposition it is. Just as no human intellect would know how to say with certainty why **Jacob of Forlì** <note>Iacobus Forliviensis (c. 1350–1414), an influential Italian physician and commentator on Galen, known for his rigorous logic.</note> and...

<margin>Healing through vows.</margin>
Regarding this same debate, one might further argue that people are not healed by miracles through their **vows** <note>original: "ex uotis"; religious promises or prayers made to God or saints in exchange for healing.</note>, but rather through a powerful **imagination** and the deep impression the patient holds regarding the physician, or through some other similar means from the various methods already assigned. For instance, there are illnesses that are incurable by their very nature, or cases where the healing occurs in a way that could not happen naturally—even if the illness itself were potentially curable. Such were the cases recorded and witnessed by **Saint Augustine** <note>A foundational Father of the Church (354–430 AD) whose later works emphasized the reality of contemporary miracles.</note>, as he himself recounts in many chapters of the twenty-second book of ***The City of God***. In short: whatever the Church has deemed a miracle must be firmly believed to be a miracle; and whatever is not so deemed should be considered not a miracle. For nothing is determined by the **Catholic Church** of God unless it proceeds from the **Word of God** and the guidance of the **Holy Spirit**.

> For what reason can someone who stays with a healthy person be made in no way sounder in body, nor can one who associates with a stronger or more beautiful person gain anything of this kind, yet someone who joins himself to a just, temperate, and good person becomes better in these very **goods of the soul**? <note>original: *bonis animi*; virtues or internal qualities of the mind/spirit as opposed to physical attributes</note>

> Or is it because we cannot change the goods of the body by means of the soul, but we can change the goods of the soul?

...learn to rejoice rightly at one moment, and to be saddened at another; a habit that cannot be acquired by one who is merely with a healthy person. Indeed, none of these things can create physical health. These are the words of Aristotle.

From these remarks, many things that have been said seem to oppose the cited opinion: First, namely, that a healthy person cannot heal another by his own health. Second, that from a healthy person there does not come forth that **evaporation** <note>original: *evaporatio*; the theory that bodies emit subtle particles or "spirits" that can affect others</note> as it does from a sick person. Third, that joy and sadness cannot cause health and sickness. Yet, the opposites of all these have been stated previously. Indeed, **Aristotle** himself <margin>Aristotle's words</margin> seems to contradict himself and go against all physicians.

Against himself, I say, as is clear from the points brought forward in the previous sections—and especially in the ninth book of the *History of Animals* concerning the **emotions of the mind** <note>original: *animi affectibus*; the passions or feelings which Pomponazzi argues have physical consequences</note>. Against the physicians, however, because by the common consensus of all medical practitioners, the **accidents of the soul** <note>original: *animi accidentia*; mental states or emotions that "happen" to a person and can shift the body's internal balance</note> are among the most significant factors contributing to health and sickness, as in the third art...

# ON INCANTATIONS
<sig>G 3</sig>

<margin>†</margin>
But this solution is not entirely satisfactory, because if sickness infects another simply because it is a "motion" <term>motion: in the Aristotelian physics used by Pomponazzi, *motus* refers to any kind of change or process, such as heating up, growing, or changing state.</term>, then whatever was a greater motion would infect more. Thus, since a fever is a "motion of alteration," it ought to infect others in its capacity as a fever—which is false (the plague excepted). Furthermore, leprosy, the itch <note>original: *scabies*; a contagious skin disease.</note>, inflammation of the eyes <note>original: *lippitudo*; a general term for various eye infections or "bleariness."</note>, and cancer do not seem to be "motions" in the same way that a fever is. Likewise, "cold" diseases <note>In the medical system of the time, diseases were classified by the four humors; "cold" diseases, like certain types of paralysis or phlegmatic illnesses, were thought to involve a lack of vital heat.</note> are in no way contagious, and yet according to your argument, they are still motions. Therefore, that solution to the Problem is doubtful.

In solving that problem, we would say that it is more difficult to produce health: for many things are required for building something up. But that contagious spirit and vapor <note>original: *spiritus ille ac uapor contagiosus*; Renaissance thinkers believed diseases were spread by "spirits" or fine vapors emitted from the body through the pores.</note> can cause sickness, for few things are sufficient for destruction. Nature is more prone toward evil <note>In this context, "evil" refers to physical deterioration or the breakdown of the body's natural order.</note> than toward good; and, as Aristotle says, one thing is enough for destruction, while many are required for construction. Therefore, evil is also more certain than good, because it arises from the necessity of nature, like death; but good is not so certain.

...while <note>Continuing the thought: "while humans exist as if secondary [to nature]..."</note> both parts are in continuous transformation; yet we can say none of these things about immaterial substances, as was demonstrated in the eighth book of the *Physics* and the second book of *On the Heavens* <note>These are two of Aristotle’s foundational works on the nature of the physical universe and the eternal motion of the stars.</note>. 

For how can immaterial and eternal beings suddenly begin to understand or desire something new? How can they be moved by physical things? How can they feel joy or sadness? These qualities, and others like them, all imply "passion" <note>original: "passionem"; in a philosophical sense, this refers to the capacity to be acted upon or changed by external forces, which Aristotle argued cannot happen to eternal, immaterial beings.</note> and a state of being subject to decay. How, too, could they speak to us, hear our voices, or see our deeds? These and similar claims seem to be nothing but delusions. This is similar to what they say Cassius told Brutus when Brutus described seeing an "evil spirit" <note>original: "malo genio"; referring to the famous legend where a phantom appeared to Brutus before the Battle of Philippi, which the Epicurean Cassius argued was merely a hallucination.</note>. 

Therefore, based both on what we have recounted and on many other arguments that could be drawn from Aristotle, such spirits—whether unclean or even good—are not accepted by the **Peripatetics** <note>Peripatetics: The name for the followers of Aristotle's school of philosophy.</note>, with the sole exception of those beings who move the celestial bodies. This concludes the first of our propositions. These points should be understood to hold if demons are not assumed to be souls...

For God ordains and disposes all things in an orderly and sweet manner <note>A reference to Wisdom 8:1: "She reacheth from one end to another mightily: and sweetly doth she order all things."</note>, and he has implanted an eternal law in things which it is impossible to bypass. That God does not act directly upon these lower things <note>The "sublunary" realm of Earth, subject to change and decay.</note> is evident from the eighth book of the *Physics*, the second book of *On the Heavens*, and the second book of the *Metaphysics*. This is because Aristotle believed that God would be changed if He acted directly; and if that were granted, God would not be God. For in Him—even according to the laws of true philosophers—no change or shadow of turning can possibly fall, as the Apostle James also testifies in his canonical epistle <note>James 1:17: "...the Father of lights, with whom is no variableness, neither shadow of turning."</note>. 
<margin>How demons or angels will act.</margin>
Therefore, Aristotle would not admit the first mode <note>The "first mode" refers to God acting directly on the world without intermediaries.</note> for the reason assigned. Let us now look at the others, namely concerning angels and demons: and I respond that we must ask how they act.

...generations differing from one another in customs and ways of life. To each one, a fixed number of years has been assigned by God, completed by the cycle of a **Great Year** <note>The "Great Year" (original: *anni magni*) is a cyclical astronomical period—often associated with the Platonic Year—after which the sun, moon, and planets return to the same relative positions.</note>. When this cycle reaches its end and another is already imminent, it is an amazing thing that a sign is moved in the earth or the sky, so that it is immediately declared to those diligently skilled in these matters that men who will follow different customs and ways of life have now been brought into the light, and who are of either greater or lesser concern to the gods than those who came before. 

Other things in this very change of generations undergo great innovations; **divination** <note>The practice of seeking knowledge of the future or the unknown by supernatural means.</note> sometimes grows with great honors and achieves its very fulfillments, since many and manifest signs are sent ahead by God himself. <meta>This page continues Pietro Pomponazzi’s discussion on the nature of omens. Having argued that God and Nature provide signs for human guidance, he now clarifies the philosophical relationship between these signs and the events they predict. He distinguishes between the "efficient cause" (the stars and nature producing the sign) and the "final cause" (the purpose of warning humanity), using both medical and military analogies to explain how a sign can indicate an event without being its direct cause.</meta>

# ON INCANTATIONS.

M 4

...either such things are the causes or the effects of things about to happen. To this we say that such signs are the effects of the heavens and nature in the category of the **efficient cause** <term>efficient cause: the primary source of change or rest; the "trigger" or "builder" that makes something happen</term>, but regarding the things that are to occur, they belong to the category of the **final cause** <term>final cause: the end, purpose, or goal for which a thing exists or is done</term>. Such a flight of ravens warns men of a future disaster. Therefore, such things have a relationship in themselves and are intended by nature for the good or ill of man. For just as among the Romans, a

purple garment placed upon a spear was a sign of an impending conflict, yet the garment did not cause the conflict, nor did the conflict cause the garment; rather, it was there for the sake of the conflict; so it is in our present subject.

# ON INCANTATIONS

...natural <note>original: "naturalibus"; completing the thought from the previous page regarding natural experiences or signs</note>, because this is not inconsistent with the works of nature. However, it must be known that it is possible for one thing to be known through another—as, for example, *b* might be known through *a*—and yet *a* is neither the cause of *b*, nor is *a* the effect of that same *b*.

<margin>One thing is known by another in various ways.</margin>

Truly, since both *a* and *b* proceed from the same cause, therefore from the knowledge of either, both can be known. For example, since the rainbow <note>original: "iris"</note> and the fair weather of the air <note>original: "serenitas aëris"</note> proceed from the same cause, we therefore judge future fair weather by the rainbow. There are, as it were, two processes at work there: the first is from the effect to the cause, when from the rainbow we proceed to the "victory over the cloud" <term>victory over the cloud: a common medieval meteorological concept where sun or heat overcomes the moisture and density of a cloud, resulting in a rainbow and eventually clear skies</term>. 

And since the victory over the cloud is the cause of the air's fair weather, we proceed from such a victory over the cloud to the fair weather of the air, just as one moves from a cause to an effect. 

<margin>The cause of fair weather and the sign.</margin>

Now, that the victory over the cloud is inferred from the rainbow, and that fair weather is inferred from the victory over the cloud, is taken for granted here as a known fact, in whatever manner it became known. Therefore, in the matter at hand, it can be said that through the chattering of a raven, future misfortune is known, because...

...alteration; <note>The text begins mid-word: "tionem," completing "alterationem" or "determinationem" from the previous page.</note> it does not change by the power of a man or a **demon**, but by its own nature. Therefore, just as it does not receive its alteration from a demon but from nature, so too it does not receive its **determination** <note>The specific direction of a force toward a particular target.</note> from one. Nevertheless, it may be determined by a demon or a man to act upon *this* specific thing. However, the fact that the object upon which it acts is determined to be something to be avoided or pursued cannot come from the person "applying" the materials. For such a person only applies <term>active things to passive ones</term> <note>original: "activa passivis"; a core principle in Aristotelian physics where change occurs when an "active" agent (like fire) meets a "passive" subject (like wood).</note>, and does not grant a new "form" or nature to the instrumental agent. 

For this is exactly as if someone—let us call him **a**—were to apply **fire** (**b**) to **wood**, so that from **b**, a new **fire** (**c**) is generated; and if that person then claimed that because fire **c** burns wood **d**, the burning was the result of the first person who applied the initial spark. To imagine such a thing is foolish. Indeed, if you consider it correctly, the argument [for demonic determination] is far worse than this example. 

Furthermore, a **demon** would be able to produce this effect no more than a **man** could; yet this is denied by those who argue for demonic power. It is manifest that this follows, however, since in this matter a demon is nothing more than one who applies active things to passive ones. <meta>This page continues Pietro Pomponazzi’s argument regarding the natural causes of what is perceived as magic. This page begins by completing the word "alteration" (alterationem) and continues his critique of those who attribute independent power to demons.</meta>

# PIETRO POMPONAZZI #

**alteration**: neither does it change through the power of a man or a **demon** <term>daemonis</term> <note>In the Renaissance, "demons" were often viewed as spiritual intermediaries capable of manipulating the physical world, but Pomponazzi argues they must follow natural laws.</note>, but from its own nature. Therefore, just as it does not derive its **alteration** from a demon but from nature, so it does not have its **determination** <note>The specific direction or "programming" of an action.</note> from them. Nevertheless, it is determined by a demon or a man to act in this specific way. 

However, the fact that the object it acts upon is determined toward one goal—either to be avoided or pursued—cannot be attributed to the "applicant" <note>The person or entity who brings two natural substances together.</note>. For the applicant only applies **active forces** to **passive ones** <term>actiua passiuis</term> <note>A fundamental principle in Aristotelian physics: change happens when an active agent meets a receptive subject.</note>, and does not grant the essential form to the **instrumental agent** <term>instrumentali</term>. 

This is exactly as if someone were to apply **a**, fire, to **b**, wood, so that from **b** a new fire **c** was generated; if one were then to say that fire **c** burns wood **d** solely because of the first person who applied the fire, it would be foolish to imagine such a thing. Indeed, if you consider it correctly, the argument for demons is far worse. 

Furthermore, a demon could not produce this effect any more than a man could—though this is denied by those who hold the opposite view. It is manifest, however, that this conclusion follows, since in this case the demon acts as nothing more than one who applies active things to passive ones. This entire process can be performed by a human being, provided there are herbs, stones, or other such natural materials available.

<vocab>Pietro Pomponazzi, demon, active, passive, instrumental, determination, power/virtue</vocab>

<keywords>naturalism, causality, demons vs. humans, active and passive principles, Aristotelian physics, instrumental agency</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Pietro Pomponazzi’s investigation into whether magical effects are caused by demons or can be explained through natural philosophy. Having previously discussed the Scholastic view that demons manipulate physical matter, he now explores the difficulty of explaining how a human mind could direct natural forces toward a specific target without supernatural aid.</meta>

-># PIETRO POMPONAZZI #<-

It is very difficult to maintain that such things are done by man and through natural means: for in my view, the greatest difficulty lies in the **determiner** <term>determinante</term> <note>In Aristotelian logic, the 'determiner' is the specific factor that directs a general natural power toward a specific target or outcome.</note>. For according to this second opinion, nothing seems able to be assigned as the determiner, except the intention of the **sorcerer** <term>malefici</term> <note>original: "malefici"; specifically one who performs harmful magic (maleficium).</note> himself; however, such an intention does not seem capable of producing such a determination, as is clear from what has been established. And I say, as it seems to me, that if it is conceded that these things can be done by **demons** <term>daemonibus</term>, it must also be believed that these things can be done by men with no demon intervening.

Therefore, perhaps someone might deny that these things are true. To this opinion <margin>Ovid denies witchcraft <note>original: "Ouidius negat ueneficia."</note></margin> **Ovid** seems to agree in his book the *Heroides*, in the *Epistle of Oenone to Paris*, where it is said: "Whatever herb is powerful for help, and whatever root useful for healing grows in all the world, is mine. Wretched me, that love is not curable by herbs; though skilled in my art, I am forsaken by my own art" <note>Ovid, *Heroides* 5.147–150. Here, the god Apollo speaks of his own inability to use medicine to solve his unrequited love for Daphne.</note>.

<margin>Things which easily lead to love or hatred</margin>

### Chapter XII. In which he responds to the proposed doubts.

<margin>
The unlearned in philosophy are not satisfied.

<margin>
What makes philosophy ridiculous.
</margin>
I know quite well that in such difficult arguments and in such hidden matters of nature, I will by no means satisfy those **unlearned in philosophy**. As to the first, then, when it is said that God and the **intelligences** <note>In the Aristotelian tradition Pomponazzi follows, "intelligences" are immaterial, eternal beings—often identified by theologians as angels—that govern the movements of the celestial spheres.</note> cannot perform such works except by willing and understanding: 

<margin>
How God understands all things.
</margin>
to this we say that it is true; but that God and the intelligences understand all things through their own essences, specifically in this way: God himself always understands himself, because he is **intellection** <note>original: *intellectio*; the pure act of thought or the state of being an intellect.</note> itself; yet he understands all other things because he is the cause of all other things. 

<margin>
How the intelligences understand.
</margin>
The other intelligences, however, first understand themselves through themselves, and in themselves they understand the higher things, since they are the effects of those higher things. This is why relics are thought to heal, even when they actually do nothing <note>Pomponazzi is first summarizing the common religious explanation: that God performs the miracle, not the physical object.</note>. Similarly, in oracles, humans do not speak or do anything, but **demons** perform such things as a result of the idolatry committed by those who desire to know what they are asking.

To this it is replied that, regarding relics, that explanation for how health is restored is not the true one.

Pomponazzi is famous for suggesting that "miracles" often have psychological, natural causes.</note>. As was seen earlier—and both **physicians and philosophers** know this—we know how much **faith** and the **imagination** of healing (or of not healing) can accomplish. 

<margin>
How much the faith of healing accomplishes.

Therefore, if these were the **bones of a dog**, and if there were such a great and powerful belief held regarding them...

...of King Pyrrhus, who was thought to possess divinity because his body could not be consumed by fire. <margin>
Thomas’s error regarding the motion of the sea.

For such a property does not follow the entire species, nor the form, but only the **matter** <note>In the Aristotelian science of the time, "form" made something what it was (e.g., a human), while "matter" was the specific physical stuff that made an individual. Indeed, in that same short treatise, the author says that the sea water is moved by the Moon in its ebb and flow, not through "impressed qualities" but just as iron is moved by a magnet. To me, this is simply not intelligible, since in every motion the mover must be in contact with the thing moved; it would require that the intervening elements also be moved according to **local motion** <note>Physical movement from one place to another through space.</note>, which is not observed to happen. Therefore, I believe that this is not his work.

### ON INCANTATIONS
<note>original: *DE INCANTATIONIB.*</note>

...comes from the power of the stars; thus, in the making of such bells, it happens that they are crafted under a specific constellation <note>In Renaissance thought, the "constellation" or alignment of stars at the moment of an object's creation determined its hidden properties.</note> that is appropriate to them. In this way, they receive much of that same influence <note>original: *influxu*. Referring to "astral influence," a literal fluid-like power believed to flow from the stars into earthly objects.</note> similar to the influence found in a herb or a stone that drives away storms. Therefore, when the bell is rung, it alters the air to such a quality that opposes the storm. If the quality induced by the bell happens to be stronger than the storm, the storm will be driven away; but if the quality is weaker, the storm will prevail, and the bell's influence will succumb. This effect on the bell could occur not only because of the impression made by the stars during its manufacture, but also from the very nature of its composition—namely, that some such [weather-repelling] substance might be included in its making.

<margin>It is not impossible for a man to be born who commands the sea.</margin>

<margin>Objection</margin>
But perhaps someone will insist, and not without reason, that the example provided was not appropriately applied, and that there is a very great difference between these things. For according to the philosophers, since **clear weather** <note>original: *serenitas*</note> is produced by the heavens, and the heavens act by **necessity** <term>necessity: the philosophical principle that certain causes must produce specific effects and cannot do otherwise</term>, then that clear weather was inevitable. 

Prayers, however, were not necessary. If they were, they would not have been meritorious, nor would it have been within the power of the **people of L’Aquila** <note>original: *Aquilani*</note> to pray—which is clearly false. Therefore, there is a disparity between these two views, and they do not share the same agreement. Indeed, what is posited according to the religious laws is consistent: for when the cause is contingent, the means, the effect, and the end are also contingent.

# ON INCANTATIONS.
<i>i</i>
<meta>catchword: diverse</meta>

...to you according to the rite of your own country; likewise, the image <note>original: "idolum"; here referring to a mental image or apparition</note> of the same thing appears to another according to the rite of his own country. Certainly no other cause can be <margin>That God disposes all things as is fitting.</margin> assigned, as Averroes <note>Ibn Rushd (1126–1198), the influential Andalusian philosopher</note> also says in his short work *On Divination through Dreams*, except that God disposes each thing as is fitting for it; otherwise He would not be a good and fitting craftsman. And this also comes from the disposition of the recipient <term>recipient: *passi*; in Aristotelian physics, the "patient" or the thing receiving an action</term>: for an Italian is affected in one way, and a Frenchman <note>original: "Gallus"</note> in another. In the second way, I say the celestial bodies are the cause of these things in themselves; <note>original: "per se"</note> but then it is not properly and truly called an **evil of fault**: <term>evil of fault: "malum culpae," referring to moral evil or sin committed by a conscious choice</term> for there can be no fault where reason cannot hold command and serve. If, however, reason is free, <note>original: "soluta," literally "loosened" or "unbound," meaning functioning independently</note> then I say that neither God nor the celestial bodies are the cause of such defects in themselves, since the will, while reason stands free, is free and can be compelled by no one. For if God were to move wills, He would move them toward the good and not toward evil; moreover, no creature can move the will by compulsion if reason is free. Therefore, in this way, neither God nor the celestial bodies are, nor can they be, the cause of evil. 

<margin>From where comes the disposition toward evil.</margin>

Sallust <note>Gaius Sallustius Crispus (86–35 BCE), a Roman historian.</note> says in the *Catiline Conspiracy* that Catiline fell into the desire to destroy his country because he had killed his own son with poison, having been captured by a love for Orestilla, who feared the son. 
<margin>The dispositions of the heavens do not necessitate.</margin>
However, that the dispositions of the heavens do not necessitate <note>In this context, "necessitate" means to force an action so that no other choice is possible.</note> human actions is clear from the reports of Albert the Great <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a medieval scholar who wrote extensively on the natural sciences.</note> in Book 1 of *On Animals*, in the treatise on Physiognomy <term>Physiognomy: the practice of assessing a person's character or fortune from their outer appearance, especially the face</term>; read there. "Indeed, it is a difficult matter to judge," etc. From this it is clear that the stars incline, but they do not compel <note>original: "astra inclinare et non cogere," a famous medieval maxim used to reconcile astrology with the Christian doctrine of free will</note>. Augustus also escaped many dangers by foreseeing his fate; Valerius Maximus reports the same in Book 1. This is what Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 CE), the most influential astronomer and astrologer of antiquity.</note> meant when he said, "The wise man will rule the stars" <note>original: "sapiens dominabitur astris"</note>. Indeed, prophecies and astrological judgments would be vain unless we were able to resist them.

<page-num>287</page-num>
<header>ON INCANTATIONS <note>original: "DE INCANTATIONIB." abbreviation for "De Incantationibus." This is the short title for Pomponazzi's work "On the Causes of Natural Effects, or On Incantations."</note></header>

it binds reason. Specifically, in those who are delirious <note>original: "phreneticis," referring to those suffering from "phrenitis," an inflammation of the brain or a state of acute mental confusion</note>, in childhood, in drunkenness, and even in decrepit old age, reason is bound: many herbs induce insanity, as do many other things. Therefore, the mind is invincible only so long as reason remains stable; otherwise, it is not. A sign of this is that because many men cannot be changed in their will, those wishing to change them make them drunk; this is evident in shameful sexual encounters <note>original: "nephandis concubitibus," literally unspeakable or heinous couplings</note> and also in the capture of women. Yet, it does not follow from this that we are compelled to sin.

<margin>That we are not compelled to sin.</margin>
For if reason is free <note>original: "soluta," literally loosened or unbound</note>, it cannot be compelled. If, however, it is bound, it is not in control of itself; therefore, it is not a sin. Just as a beast is not said to sin, because it does not have the use of reason.

<margin>Regarding the seventh doubt.</margin>
The "sin" of which we speak does not exist except in one who is able to use reason.

### Chapter 13. In which is set forth what we definitively think, by presenting several points in the form of conclusions.

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
Those who, according to the mind of Aristotle, posit any immaterial substances besides the intelligences <note>In medieval philosophy, "Intelligences" were spiritual beings thought to move the celestial spheres/planets.</note> that move the celestial spheres, are by no means to be called Aristotelians; rather, let them be considered entirely foreign to his doctrine. 

<margin>That angels or demons do not exist according to Aristotle.</margin>
This conclusion is manifest: first, from his opinion in the 12th book of the *Metaphysics*, in which that point is most clearly set down. Second, it is confirmed by reason, since such substances, being perpetual and intelligent, are not corporeal animals possessing senses, as Aristotle himself strives to show at the end of the third book of *On the Soul* <note>original: *De Anima*</note>. It is therefore necessary, according to him, that they possess only intellect and desire among the powers of the soul; they are, therefore, entirely abstract and immobile. 

The question then arises whether such beings are posited because of some observed phenomenon <note>original: *apparente*. A technical term for an empirical observation that needs an explanation.</note> that cannot be accounted for <note>original: *salvari*. Literally "saved," referring to the scientific principle of "saving the appearances."</note> without their existence, or whether they are posited without any reason. The second option is not only foreign to all scientific weight <note>original: *physica gravitate*. Meaning philosophical or intellectual seriousness.</note>, but indeed [should be rejected] by anyone who [does not wish] to be considered vain and empty...

He asserts that any philosopher claiming otherwise is not a true Aristotelian and that such beings are not necessary to explain natural phenomena.</summary>

<margin>Second conclusion.</margin> The second conclusion is this: regarding the effects which people commonly attribute to demons—and indeed even to good angels—in cases where God does not intervene in a special and proper way, but only according to his general way <note>In Scholastic philosophy, "general way" refers to God sustaining the natural laws of the universe, whereas "special way" refers to direct miracles that bypass those laws.</note>, even setting aside the authority of Aristotle, it cannot be effectively proven that such immaterial substances exist. This conclusion is proven in many ways: first, because those things which are supposedly produced by angels or demons are achieved either by **alteration** <note>original: "alterando"; in Aristotelian physics, this refers to a change in the quality of a substance, such as heating or cooling.</note>, or by **local motion** <note>original: "localiter mouendo"; the physical movement of an object from one place to another.</note>, or by both methods. It is not proven by alteration, for as is commonly held—and it is the opinion of **Augustine** in the third book of *On the Trinity* <note>original: "August. in 3. de Trinitate"</note>—immaterial substances, with the exception of God, cannot cause immediate alteration; instead, only bodies and natural beings can cause alteration. <margin>Second conclusion.</margin> **The second conclusion** is this: Regarding the effects that people commonly attribute to demons, or even to good angels—excluding those where God intervenes in a special and specific way, and considering only His general influence—even if we set aside the authority of Aristotle, it cannot be effectively proven that such **immaterial substances** <note>Substances that exist without physical matter, such as spirits or souls.</note> exist. 

This conclusion is proven in several ways. First, because the things that are reportedly done by angels or demons are achieved either by **altering** a substance, by **moving** it from place to place, or by both methods. However, none of these effects force us to accept [a supernatural cause].

Instead, they can only alter physical bodies and natural beings [by using other physical tools]. Therefore, for the process of **alteration** <note>In Aristotelian physics, "alteration" refers to a change in quality, such as heating or cooling, rather than a change in location.</note> itself, the "lower bodies" <note>The four elements and terrestrial matter.</note> acting together with the **celestial bodies** <note>The stars and planets, believed in this period to be the primary active forces in the universe.</note> are sufficient.

Moreover, according to the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle, known for seeking natural and logical causes for all phenomena.</note>, this cannot be said, as is self-evident. Therefore, there seems to be no compelling reason—nor even a rational discovery—to grant that such spirits <note>referring to the demons or angels mentioned on the previous page</note> are necessary. I say, then, that it is not true that the force moving the minds of those who are prophesying <note>original: *vaticinantes*</note> in their sleep must touch those minds directly. Instead, it is enough for the force to reach them through a power impressed upon the air by the celestial bodies. Yet, the celestial bodies (or their spiritual forms) are not themselves moved or affected in any way by the people who are dreaming. Rather, such a movement occurs simply because the active and passive factors <note>The "active" celestial influence and the "passive" human mind or body that is ready to receive it.</note> were suitably aligned at that moment, and not before. Nor is a specific, individual connection required at that time, but only a universal influence, which is nevertheless determined for a specific "here and now." ->CONCLUSION<-

You have therefore, most dear companion <note>original: *compater*; literally "godfather," used here as a term of endearment for his friend or patron, likely the person who commissioned the work</note>, those things which, as my opinion holds, the **Peripatetics** <term>Peripatetics: followers of Aristotle's philosophical school, named after the covered walkways (peripatos) where they walked while debating</term> would likely have to say regarding the things you have asked. <margin>He submits himself to the judgment of the Church.</margin>
As far as religion is concerned, if anything in these words of ours is found offensive, which is contrary to the **Holy Catholic Church**, or is displeasing to it, I revoke all of that, and I humbly submit myself to its correction. In those matters, however, which pertain to the Peripatetic discipline, I desire that which **Aristotle** reports in the last chapter of the sixth [book] of the *Topics* <note>Aristotle’s *Topica* is a treatise on the art of dialectical argument; the author is appealing to the standards of academic debate.</note> concerning Agreements to be observed: until something better than these [arguments] appears.

<meta>This page concludes Pietro Pomponazzi’s "De Incantationibus" (On Incantations). This final section emphasizes the cumulative nature of knowledge and ends with a formal prayer and signature.</meta>

# PIETRO POMPONAZZI

...should yield: because when a better argument appears, the former should yield. Thus I also think it ought to be maintained, so that our responses might hold for as long as better ones are not found. For I have received nothing more true in this matter than something from others.

<margin>The difficulty of the work.</margin>
However, it is difficult to discover and to perfect. Therefore, let it be enough to have discovered, even if I have not perfected. For sciences come about through cumulative additions. And if **Phrynis** had not existed, neither would **Timotheus** have existed, as is written in the second book of the **Metaphysics** <note>Aristotle uses these two musicians—Phrynis and his student Timotheus—to illustrate that knowledge is built upon the contributions of predecessors. Even "wrong" or "lesser" thinkers provide the foundation for later perfection.</note>.

<margin>He gives thanks to God.</margin>
Moreover, for all things, let infinite thanks be given to Him who can exist without all things: yet nothing without Him can either exist or be imagined: from whom all things come, and He Himself from no one: toward whom all things are ordered: and He Himself is ordered toward nothing: for He is the **alpha and omega** <note>original: "alpha & ω"; the first and last letters of the Greek alphabet, symbolizing the beginning and the end</note>, the beginning, namely, and the end: but before the beginning there is nothing: after the end there is no end, who is God, blessed forever and ever.

Thus this **study** <term>original: *lucubratio*; literally "work done by lamplight," implying intense nighttime scholarly labor</term> of ours is completed, which can be titled *On Incantations*, by me, **Pietro**, son of Giovanni Niccolò Pomponazzi of Mantua, in

<meta>catchword: ni, in</meta>

<summary>Pomponazzi concludes his treatise by acknowledging that scientific progress is a collaborative effort over generations and offers a final prayer of thanks to God as the source and end of all things. He ends by identifying himself and the title of the work, *On Incantations*.</summary>
